items.stem: Which of the following questions is mainly about consequence?
options: What were the effects of the Treaty of Versailles on the Weimar Republic?
Why did the First World War break out in 1914?
Why do historians disagree about Stalin?
How far did Russian peasant life stay the same after 1861?
items.answer: What were the effects of the Treaty of Versailles on the Weimar Republic?
items.markingKey: A. Asking about effects or results of an event is the concept of consequence.

items.stem: A student claims that the concept of perspectives only concerns the opinions of modern historians. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Perspectives include the viewpoints of contemporaries in the past (victims, perpetrators, bystanders, governments) as well as later historians’ interpretations.
items.markingKey: Perspectives include the viewpoints of contemporaries in the past (victims, perpetrators, bystanders, governments) as well as later historians’ interpretations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between causation and consequence.
items.answer: Causation looks backwards to why an event happened; consequence looks forwards to what resulted from it, though one event’s consequences often become causes of later events.
items.markingKey: Causation looks backwards to why an event happened; consequence looks forwards to what resulted from it, though one event’s consequences often become causes of later events. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source C: E. H. Carr, a British historian of Soviet Russia, in What is History?, the published version of his Trevelyan Lectures at Cambridge, 1961 (adapted)

“The facts speak only when the historian calls on them: it is he who decides to which facts to give the floor, and in what order or context.” History, Carr argues, is a continuous process of interaction between the historian and his facts, an unending dialogue between the present and the past.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for an historian studying how historians construct knowledge about the past.
items.answer: Value: It is a classic, widely debated statement by an experienced professional historian, written to provoke reflection on historical method; it shows how the selection of evidence shapes interpretation. Limitations: It is a theoretical argument rather than evidence about any event; Carr wrote as a Marxist-influenced liberal reacting against empiricist historians such as G. R. Elton, so he may overstate the subjectivity of history.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the concept of perspectives makes objective historical knowledge impossible.
items.answer: Perspectives limit claims to absolute objectivity but rigorous method allows reliable, if provisional, knowledge.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: historians select evidence and frame questions from their own present (Carr); national narratives of the same event differ sharply. Arguments against: methods of corroboration and peer review limit bias; some facts (dates, documented events) are not in dispute; recognising perspectives is itself a means to a more complete understanding. Supported judgement: Perspectives limit claims to absolute objectivity but rigorous method allows reliable, if provisional, knowledge.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "consequence".
items.answer: An outcome or result of an event or development, which may be intended or unintended, short-term or long-term

items.stem:
Source B: E. H. Carr, a British historian of Soviet Russia, in What is History?, the published version of his Trevelyan Lectures at Cambridge, 1961 (adapted)

“The facts speak only when the historian calls on them: it is he who decides to which facts to give the floor, and in what order or context.” History, Carr argues, is a continuous process of interaction between the historian and his facts, an unending dialogue between the present and the past.

items.answer: History is not a set of facts that speaks for itself; historians select and order the facts, so historical knowledge is shaped by the historian and by the present in which he or she writes.

Source B: Marc Bloch, French historian and co-founder of the Annales school, The Historian’s Craft, written in 1941–1944 while in the Resistance and published posthumously in 1949 (adapted translation)

Misunderstanding of the present is the inevitable consequence of ignorance of the past. But a man may wear himself out just as fruitlessly in seeking to understand the past, if he is totally ignorant of the present.

In what ways do Sources A and B agree and disagree about how historians construct knowledge about the past?
items.answer: Both argue that historians are not passive recorders of facts and that the present shapes the study of the past. Carr stresses the historian’s selection of facts and the subjectivity this creates, whereas Bloch stresses the two-way usefulness of past and present for understanding each other; Carr questions objectivity more directly.

items.stem: Using the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 as an example, explain the way one event can be both a consequence and a cause.
items.answer: US share prices collapsed, banks failed and American loans to Europe were recalled, deepening the global Depression. The Crash was a consequence of speculation and over-production, and itself became a cause of mass unemployment in Germany that helped the Nazis win 37% of the vote in July 1932.

Source A: Summary of the argument of Fritz Fischer, German historian, Griff nach der Weltmacht (Germany’s Aims in the First World War), 1961 (paraphrased)

The German government’s “blank cheque” of 5–6 July 1914 promised Austria-Hungary unconditional support against Serbia. Berlin’s leaders accepted the risk of a continental war, believing that time was running against Germany as Russia rearmed.

An historian is researching the causes of major historical events. Explain the value and limitations of Source A for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.
items.answer: Value: Fischer used extensive German archival evidence and his thesis transformed the debate; useful for showing a deliberate-policy explanation of causes. Limitations: Written by a German historian challenging his own nation’s post-war consensus, it was highly controversial; it focuses on German decisions and may under-weight the roles of Russia, France and Britain.

items.answer: Proximity in time does not equal importance: the immediate event is often a trigger working on deeper, long-term conditions.

The statesmen of 1914 were sleepwalkers, watchful but unseeing, haunted by dreams, yet blind to the reality of the horror they were about to bring into the world. The outbreak of war was a tragedy, not a crime.

To what extent do Sources A and B present a similar picture of the causes of major historical events?
items.answer: Both focus on decisions by political leaders in July 1914. items.stem: Briefly describe the Cuban Revolution of 1959 and explain what it reveals about multi-causal explanation.

items.stem: Using the commemoration of the Rwandan genocide each April (Kwibuka) as an example, explain how significance is constructed through memory.
items.answer: Rwanda holds 100 days of remembrance from 7 April, centred on memorial sites such as Kigali Genocide Memorial. The state uses commemoration to present the genocide as the defining event of the nation’s history, shaping national identity and policy.
items.markingKey: Context (Rwanda holds 100 days of remembrance from 7 April, centred on memorial sites such as Kigali Genocide Memorial.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The state uses commemoration to present the genocide as the defining event of the nation’s history, shaping national identity and policy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how significance is constructed through memory.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the argument that the outbreak of the First World War was primarily the result of German policy.
items.answer: German decisions were crucial, but responsibility was shared in a complex crisis.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: blank cheque of July 1914 (Fischer); Schlieffen Plan required the invasion of Belgium; Russian general mobilisation on 30 July; Austria-Hungary’s ultimatum to Serbia; alliance commitments and shared miscalculation (Clark). A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: German decisions were crucial, but responsibility was shared in a complex crisis. Markbands – 13–15: clearly focused, well structured response; accurate and relevant knowledge used effectively; well-chosen examples; evaluation of different perspectives; all main points substantiated; reasoned, consistent conclusion; 10–12: clear awareness of the demands; clearly structured; accurate, relevant knowledge placed in context; analysis with most points substantiated; some awareness of different perspectives; 7–9: demands understood but not all implications considered; mostly accurate knowledge; some critical analysis, though partly narrative; 4–6: some indication of the demands; some knowledge but lacking accuracy or relevance; mostly narrative or descriptive, limited analysis; 1–3: little understanding of the demands of the question; poorly structured, little relevant knowledge, no analysis; 0: does not reach the standard of the descriptors below.

items.stem:
Source A: E. H. Carr, a British historian of Soviet Russia, in What is History?, the published version of his Trevelyan Lectures at Cambridge, 1961 (adapted)

“The facts speak only when the historian calls on them: it is he who decides to which facts to give the floor, and in what order or context.” History, Carr argues, is a continuous process of interaction between the historian and his facts, an unending dialogue between the present and the past.

Source B: Marc Bloch, French historian and co-founder of the Annales school, The Historian’s Craft, written in 1941–1944 while in the Resistance and published posthumously in 1949 (adapted translation)

Misunderstanding of the present is the inevitable consequence of ignorance of the past. But a man may wear himself out just as fruitlessly in seeking to understand the past, if he is totally ignorant of the present.

Using the sources and your own knowledge, discuss the view that the concept of perspectives makes objective historical knowledge impossible.
items.answer: Perspectives limit claims to absolute objectivity but rigorous method allows reliable, if provisional, knowledge.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: historians select evidence and frame questions from their own present (Carr); national narratives of the same event differ sharply. Challenging: methods of corroboration and peer review limit bias; some facts (dates, documented events) are not in dispute; recognising perspectives is itself a means to a more complete understanding. Judgement: Perspectives limit claims to absolute objectivity but rigorous method allows reliable, if provisional, knowledge. Candidates must use both sources and their own knowledge; Markbands – 6–8: focused response; effective use of the sources and accurate own knowledge, integrated (synthesised) to support a clear, balanced judgement; 4–5: some focus on the question; uses sources or own knowledge, with some analysis but little synthesis; 1–3: limited understanding; generalised comments, sources or own knowledge used descriptively; 0: does not reach the standard of the descriptors below.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Richard Overy, British historian, Why the Allies Won, 1995

The decisive factor was not one battle but the Soviet capacity to out-produce Germany: by 1943 the USSR was building more tanks and aircraft than the Reich, with Lend-Lease supplies providing trucks and food.

Source B: Adapted from Antony Beevor, British military historian, Stalingrad, 1998

After Stalingrad the soldiers of the Red Army knew that the Germans could be beaten. Hitler lost an entire army, and the myth of German invincibility was shattered. From this point the initiative passed to the Soviet side.

With reference to both sources and your own knowledge, assess the validity of the argument that the extent of change after a revolution is usually less than revolutionaries claim.
items.answer: Revolutions often bring deep political change but significant continuity in economic structures and methods of rule.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: continuity of authoritarian rule after 1917 in Russia; Cuba retained dependence on sugar exports after 1959. Challenging: land reform and nationalisation in Cuba transformed ownership; Chinese communist rule after 1949 transformed social structures. Judgement: Revolutions often bring deep political change but significant continuity in economic structures and methods of rule. items.stem: Which of the following describes a necessary cause?
options: The event that occurred immediately before
A factor without which the event could not have happened
A factor identified by most historians
A factor that guaranteed the event would happen
items.answer: A factor without which the event could not have happened
items.markingKey: B. Necessary causes are preconditions; they need not be sufficient.

items.stem: A historian argues that peasant life in rural Russia altered very little between 1861 and 1917. Which of the following key concepts is the focus of this argument?
items.answer: Continuity
items.markingKey: A. The claim is about persistence across a period, i.e. continuity.

items.stem: Distinguish between revolutionary change and evolutionary change.
items.answer: Evolutionary change is gradual and builds on existing structures; revolutionary change is a rapid rupture that overturns them.
items.markingKey: Evolutionary change is gradual and builds on existing structures; revolutionary change is a rapid rupture that overturns them. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "An event is significant only if it caused a war or revolution." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Significance may also lie in what an event reveals about a society, its long-term effects, or its importance in memory and identity.
items.markingKey: Significance may also lie in what an event reveals about a society, its long-term effects, or its importance in memory and identity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a good causation essay explains each cause in a separate paragraph and then stops. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A strong answer also shows how causes interacted and reaches a supported judgement about their relative importance.
items.markingKey: A strong answer also shows how causes interacted and reaches a supported judgement about their relative importance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that continuity means that nothing happened during a period. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Continuity means that certain features persisted; many events may occur while structures, beliefs or living standards remain broadly the same.
items.markingKey: Continuity means that certain features persisted; many events may occur while structures, beliefs or living standards remain broadly the same. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why historians often disagree about whether an event was a turning point.
items.answer: They use different criteria and time-scales, focus on different groups, and may see the event as accelerating trends that had already begun rather than reversing them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They use different criteria and time-scales, focus on different groups, and may see the event as accelerating trends that had already begun rather than reversing them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from a survey of Cold War historiography in John Lewis Gaddis, We Now Know: Rethinking Cold War History, 1997

Historians, writing at the height of the Cold War, saw Soviet expansion as the cause of the conflict. A generation later, angered by Vietnam, others turned the question around and asked what drove American policy. Each generation writes its own history.

An historian is researching why historians disagree and how significance is judged. Explain the value and limitations of Source A for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.
items.answer: Value: Written by a leading historian of the Cold War, after the opening of some Soviet bloc archives, it gives an overview of how interpretations developed. Limitations: Gaddis is himself a participant in the debate (later called neo-orthodox), so his summary of other schools may be selective; it is a secondary overview, not evidence of events.

items.stem:
Source C: Summary of the argument of Fritz Fischer, German historian, Griff nach der Weltmacht (Germany’s Aims in the First World War), 1961 (paraphrased)

The German government’s “blank cheque” of 5–6 July 1914 promised Austria-Hungary unconditional support against Serbia. Berlin’s leaders accepted the risk of a continental war, believing that time was running against Germany as Russia rearmed.

Explain the view of the causes of major historical events that is presented in Source C.
items.answer: Germany bears major responsibility for the war: its leaders deliberately backed Austria and accepted the risk of a wider war because they feared Russian power was growing.
items.markingKey: Germany bears major responsibility for the war: its leaders deliberately backed Austria and accepted the risk of a wider war because they feared Russian power was growing. Source B: Marc Bloch, French historian and co-founder of the Annales school, The Historian’s Craft, written in 1941–1944 while in the Resistance and published posthumously in 1949 (adapted translation)

Misunderstanding of the present is the inevitable consequence of ignorance of the past. But a man may wear himself out just as fruitlessly in seeking to understand the past, if he is totally ignorant of the present.

How far can Source B be trusted as evidence for how historians construct knowledge about the past? Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source.
items.answer: Value: Bloch was a leading professional historian reflecting on method; written during the Second World War, it shows how the historian’s present shapes questions asked of the past. Limitations: It was unfinished and published after his execution in 1944, edited by Lucien Febvre; it is a reflective essay, not a systematic account, and its wartime context may shape its emphasis.

items.stem:
Source B: Paraphrased from Peter Seixas and Tom Morton, Canadian historians of education, The Big Six Historical Thinking Concepts, 2013

The importance of an event lies not only in its immediate effects but in what it reveals: the debate about a past event often tells us as much about the society remembering it as about the event itself.

What is the message of Source B about why historians disagree and how significance is judged?
items.answer: Significance is constructed: events become important because of their effects and because of what they reveal and how societies remember them.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that causation is the most important of the six key concepts for historians.
items.answer: Causation is central but cannot be separated from the other concepts; its importance depends on the question asked.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explaining why events happen is central to most historical questions; judgements about causes underpin debates such as the origins of the Second World War or the Rwandan genocide. Arguments against: significance and perspectives determine which causes historians even investigate; change and continuity questions are equally central, e.g. assessing the impact of a revolution; the concepts are interdependent, so ranking them is artificial. Supported judgement: Causation is central but cannot be separated from the other concepts; its importance depends on the question asked. Markbands: Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands, scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, accurate and relevant knowledge used to support critical analysis, different perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – little understanding of the demands, mainly description.
